newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin ends long tradition with civilian minister.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin ends long tradition with civilian minister.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's decision on Wednesday to switch to civilian defence ministers has ended decades of tradition and opened the way for radical changes in the running of Russia's armed forces.
Yeltsin issued an order retiring Igor Rodionov from military service, days after his 60th birthday, but said he would remain defence minister.

The move, long sought by Western governments, ended a tradition of generals running the ministry that dated back to Soviet times and paved the way for Russia's first civilian defence minister since the Bolshevik Revolution.

"The experience of democratic states testifies that a civilian standing at the helm of the ministry of defence can successfully tackle the whole set of problems of strengthening the state's defence potential and ensuring the vital activity of the army and navy," Yeltsin told Interfax and RIA news agencies.

Moscow's Military History Institute said Russia's last civilian defence minister was Leon Trotsky, who was appointed People's Commissar for Military and Naval Affairs in 1918, the year after the Bolshevik Revolution.

One Soviet defence minister, Dmitry Ustinov, was a civilian arms industry veteran when he was appointed in the 1970s. But Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev soon gave him the rank of Marshal and he regularly appeared in army uniform.

Military experts expected Yeltsin's move to be followed by a clear division of functions between the defence minister, who would be responsible for political matters, and the chief of the general staff, who would deal with military organisation.
Yeltsin's advisory Defence Council said after meeting on Wednesday that such a division of duties was being considered.

"The president's decision will lead to radical reorganisation of the whole system of running the structures in the armed forces," Alexander Zhilin, defence analyst for the weekly newspaper Moscow News, told Reuters.

"The defence minister will carry out political functions, being less like a general than a politician or a civil servant. The chief of the general staff will not be involved in politics and will deal with purely military matters."

Rodionov's duties look set to include responsibility for financial matters, political decisions, working out military doctrine, restructuring the army and relations with politicians, the Kremlin and the general public.

Defence experts expect General Viktor Samsonov, the chief of the general staff, to be given command of all Russian troops. Until now the defence, interior and emergencies ministries have controlled their own troops.

"The idea is that the chief of the general staff takes charge of all the troops," said Andrei Piontkowsky, head of Moscow's Centre for Strategic Studies. "This is very important for coordinating them."
He praised Wednesday's decision as a "transition" preparing the way for a minister from a purely civilian background and making Russia's defence structures compatible with the West's.

"The army needs time to learn it has a civilian defence minister. Rodionov will be a 'military civilian minister'. After him there will be a purely civilian minister," said Vladimir Lukin, head of parliament's foreign affairs committee.
Some experts cast doubts on Yeltsin's move because Rodionov could not be considered a true civilian.

"I think the defence ministry does need a civilian minister ...but if Rodionov takes off his green army jacket, he does not become such an expert. This is window-dressing," said Pavel Felgengauer, a defence analyst with Sevodnya newspaper.
Viktor Ilyukhin, head of parliament's security committee, said the move would weaken discipline in the armed forces.
Once the pride of the Soviet Union, Moscow's armed forces are now so underfunded and demoralised that Rodionov has several times had to put down talk of an army mutiny.
A major consideration is whether the changes will boost reforms intended to reduce the army and make it more efficient.
"It must help reforms because each person will be able to deal just with his own concerns," Zhilin said, adding that the army might also cease to be the subject of political intrigues.

Nikolai Bezborodov, deputy head of parliament's defence committee agreed. "We must divide the functions of the chief of the general staff and the defence minister. If changes go in this direction, what has happened is a positive thing," he said.
"In this case, we will consider that reform from above has already started in the armed forces."
